paras: The Pell City mob attack occurred on Saturday, July 18, 1903, near Pell City, St. Clair County, Alabama, when a crowd of thirty or more white men chased a Black man to his home, fired on it, and that night burned a neighboring Black family's dwelling. The man and a child were wounded, two of the white pursuers were shot, and the burned-out family was left homeless. It drew notice because Judge A. H. Alston summoned a special grand jury and denounced the burning, a charge two Alabama dailies reprinted and praised.

The trouble began at a baseball game between Ashville and Pell City, according to H. Clay Davis of Anniston, who spent the day there and said "factory hands" had quarreled with the man. Judge Alston's account was more specific: the man, known as "goosey," had been "goosed" by young white men while holding a rock, which he threw down and which struck one of them.

The man ran, and a crowd of thirty or more white men, several of them drunk, pursued him. The sheriff was present and urged the crowd to desist, but according to the charge "his remonstractions were met with oaths" and the chase went on. Reaching his home, the man took up a rifle and warned the crowd not to advance; when they came on and fired at him, he fired back and wounded two of them.

Shots fired into the house wounded a child, and the man himself was slightly wounded before he escaped. About 10 o'clock that night the mob returned and, failing to find him, set fire to an adjacent dwelling occupied by a Black family "in no way connected with the man." The family lost everything they owned. Davis reported that no "lynching bee" had been heard of, though that "seemed to be the purpose of the mob."

Judge A. H. Alston, a supernumerary judge presiding over the circuit court at Pell City, ordered a special grand jury summoned, the regular grand jury having already adjourned. In his charge he described a heap of ashes near the courthouse left by "a lawless and violent mob," explained that burning a dwelling was first-degree arson punishable by death or at least ten years in prison, and told the jurors to find who had committed "this cruel and cowardly crime." He framed this as a duty of white rule: Black people "have been disfranchised by us" and were "helpless and absolutely dependent" on whites for protection.
The Age-Herald and the Montgomery Advertiser expected action or indictments, but no report of the grand jury's findings, of arrests or of a trial was found.

All the coverage found came from two white dailies, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Montgomery Advertiser; no Black-press report was found. The Age-Herald's first report, an Anniston special, was headlined "NEGRO'S HOUSE IS BURNED BY WHITES" and "CROWD AFTER VENGEANCE." Its Pell City report of July 24, headed "ALSTON TELLS THE JURY OF A CRIME," called the episode a riot and printed the charge under the subhead "Defense of a Home."

Editorially the Age-Herald called the attackers "lynchers," blamed their energy on "moonshine," and wrote that "If every southern circuit had such a judge lynching bees would quickly disappear." A one-line item on July 27 added that "The frisky lyncher is up against Judge Alston." The Montgomery Advertiser reprinted the charge's account of the attack on July 29 and praised the judge for seeking to "impress upon the superior white race its duties towards the inferior, helpless, weaker race." The charge was also quoted in a peonage trial reported by the Advertiser on July 25.

The two accounts differ on whose house burned. Davis, reporting secondhand, said it was the pursued man's own house, a mile out on the road to Sedden, burned by friends of the wounded men, and that he had already fled with another Black man. Judge Alston's charge, given in court at Pell City, said the man exchanged fire at home and that the house burned at 10 p.m. belonged to an unconnected neighboring family; as the later, local and official account it is the fuller version.

accounts.label: Anniston correspondent relaying H. Clay Davis
accounts.gist: A quarrel at the ball game led factory hands to chase the man home, where he shot two of them with a Winchester; friends of the wounded fired shots and burned his own house, but he had fled with another Black man.

accounts.label: Judge Alston's charge to the special grand jury
accounts.gist: The man, 'goosed' by young white men, dropped a rock that struck one; thirty or more pursued him over the sheriff's objection, fired on his home and wounded him and a child after he wounded two; at 10 p.m. the mob returned and burned an unconnected neighbor family's house.

framing.detail: First report headlined 'NEGRO'S HOUSE IS BURNED BY WHITES' and 'CROWD AFTER VENGEANCE', with the man's shooting of two white men in the deck.

Age-Herald news report 'ALSTON TELLS THE JURY OF A CRIME', 'ACTION OF MOB CENSURED', calling it a riot and the attack 'uncalled for' and 'cowardly'; its editorials called the attackers 'lynchers' fueled by moonshine.
The Advertiser condemned the mob and expected indictments but praised the judge for impressing on 'the superior white race its duties towards the inferior, helpless, weaker race'.
